strengths: Well-motivated problem with formal theoretical foundation (Theorem 1 proving uniqueness of MAD solution)
Addresses genuine limitation of prior work by supporting asymmetric distances via quasimetrics, a meaningful improvement over symmetric metric approaches

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across diverse environments (deterministic/stochastic, discrete/continuous, noisy, asymmetric dynamics) with multiple metrics (Spearman, Pearson, Ratio CV)
Strong empirical results showing MadDist achieves near-perfect performance (1.00±0.00) across multiple benchmarks and translates to superior downstream planning performance
Extensive reproducibility information with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and benchmark specifications in appendices
Thorough ablations examining latent dimension, quasimetric choice, and dataset size effects
Novel benchmark suite with known/approximated ground-truth MAD values enabling systematic evaluation
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: MadDist is incremental refinement of Steccanella & Jonsson (2022) combining scale-invariant loss, quasimetric replacement, and contrastive term; TDMadDist applies standard temporal difference bootstrapping
Inconsistent contribution: TDMadDist consistently underperforms MadDist (Figs 3, Table 1) with inadequately explained underperformance, raising questions about its inclusion as main result

Quasimetric theoretical analysis insufficient: d_simple lacks deep justification beyond satisfying quasimetric axioms; limited explanation for why simple weighted average outperforms structured alternatives (IQE, WideNorm)
Ground truth MAD for continuous environments only approximated via discretization+Floyd-Warshall; approximation quality never quantified, undermining confidence in evaluation validity

Incomplete stochasticity handling: MAD based on transition support is only lower bound in stochastic settings; no systematic exploration of approximation failure modes; Stochastic Shortest Path comparison deferred
Critical ablations missing: no isolation of individual loss term impacts (L_o, L_r, L_c), weight w_r not ablated, constraint cutoff H_c (default 6) unjustified without sensitivity analysis
Limited baseline comparisons: only QRL and Hilbert included; missing bisimulation-based, contrastive, and Laplacian-based methods mentioned in related work

Downstream evaluation limitations: planning uses only random shooting (weak baseline); no full goal-conditioned RL agents; improvements sometimes marginal (Hilbert baseline achieving 0.01 success suggests implementation concerns)
Asymmetry contribution not fully justified: most environments lack strong irreversibility; limited analysis of which problem classes benefit from asymmetric modeling
Hyperparameter sensitivity understudied: multiple hyperparameters (w_r, d_max, H_c, etc.) with no principled selection guidance; limited sensitivity analysis

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation suite with diverse environments (discrete/continuous state spaces, stochastic/deterministic dynamics, asymmetric transitions, noisy observations) provides valuable benchmark
Clear problem formulation and principled approach to asymmetry via quasimetrics addresses real limitation of prior symmetric distance methods
Strong empirical results on representation learning metrics (Figures 3, 9-11) and downstream planning tasks (Table 1)
Extensive reproducibility materials including full hyperparameters, implementation details, and ablation studies (latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size)
Rigorous theoretical foundation with proof of MAD uniqueness (Appendix A) and mathematical analysis of quasimetric properties (Appendix B)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: MadDist is incremental modification of Steccanella & Jonsson (2022) with ad-hoc loss term combinations; TDMadDist applies standard TD bootstrapping and significantly underperforms MadDist in many settings (Figures 3, 9-11), questioning its value as contribution

Experimental fairness concerns: QRL baseline uses environment-specific hyperparameter tuning (α,β) with unclear optimization parity; Hilbert baseline is inherently symmetric making comparison unfair; missing symmetric version of proposed method as proper ablation

Incomplete downstream evaluation: Only planning task demonstrated despite motivation for goal-conditioned RL and reward shaping; planning uses true simulator and random action sampling, limiting practical relevance

Insufficient theoretical analysis of quasimetric design: Simple quasimetric (Eq. 3) empirically best but lacks intuition or analysis of why; no verification that learned embeddings satisfy quasimetric properties; benefits appear across symmetric/asymmetric environments despite asymmetry being positioned as key advantage

Overstated stochasticity robustness: Evaluated primarily on observation noise and sparse action failures, not truly stochastic environments; MAD becomes lower bound approximation in high-stochasticity regimes but failure modes unexplored

Misleading continuous state space claims: Ground-truth computed via maze discretization and Floyd-Warshall, making it approximate not exact; discretization error impact unquantified; 'continuous' observations mask discrete underlying structure

Missing critical ablations: No sensitivity analysis for constraint horizon Hc=6, contrastive loss hyperparameter dmax∈{100,500}; TDMadDist underperformance not investigated; no symmetric vs. asymmetric distance comparison within same algorithm

No convergence analysis or sample complexity bounds; no characterization of approximation error between learned distances and true MAD; loss function design (Eq. 4-7) appears ad-hoc without justification for specific term combinations
Reproducibility gaps: No code availability mentioned; sensitivity to initial data coverage largely unexamined; practical data requirements unclear for real applications

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear applications in goal-conditioned RL and reward shaping; the shift to quasimetrics for capturing asymmetric MAD is technically sound and well-justified
Rigorous theoretical foundation with a clean uniqueness proof for the MAD optimization problem and clear connection to shortest-path formulations

Comprehensive and diverse experimental evaluation spanning discrete/continuous spaces, deterministic/stochastic dynamics, symmetric/asymmetric transitions, and noisy observations with proper statistical rigor (3-5 seeds, error bars)
Novel simple quasimetric function (dsimple) that is both elegant and empirically superior to more complex alternatives, with systematic ablations demonstrating robustness
Valuable benchmark suite with known ground-truth MAD values enabling controlled evaluation of future methods; includes qualitative visualizations demonstrating learned geometry
Strong empirical results with MadDist consistently outperforming baselines, particularly impressive in asymmetric environments; planning experiments demonstrate practical utility
Exceptional reproducibility with thorough implementation details, complete hyperparameter specifications, and detailed environment descriptions across extensive appendices
weaknesses: TDMadDist consistently underperforms MadDist despite being theoretically well-motivated with temporal-difference learning; explanation is vague and post-hoc, raising questions about whether bootstrapping actually helps for this problem
Constraint loss (Lc) only enforces upper bounds for j-i ≤ Hc=6 without justification; this is rarely active in long-horizon environments but no ablation study examines its impact or optimal value

Scale-invariant loss in Eq. 5 may have issues: dividing by (j-i) magnifies small-distance errors and suppresses large-distance errors in ways not well-justified; alternative scale-invariant formulations not considered

Somewhat incremental novelty: core idea of learning MAD from trajectories exists in prior work (Steccanella & Jonsson 2022, Park et al. 2024b); main contributions are quasimetric support, loss design, and benchmarks rather than fundamental methodological innovations

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: Hilbert baseline is fundamentally designed for symmetric distances; unclear if QRL hyperparameter tuning was equally extensive; could baselines be extended to use asymmetric distances?

Planning experiments use weak baselines (random shooting with K=100; for AntMaze, dataset-conditioned selection is quasi-imitation learning); more sophisticated planners (e.g., A* with learned distance heuristic) would be more convincing
Extensive hyperparameter sensitivity (wr, wc, dmax, Hc, τ) with incomplete ablations; choice of dmax∈{100,500} not justified; Table 2-3 complexity raises questions about generalization to new domains

Limited exploration of practical utility: only two downstream applications tested; paper would be strengthened by more extensive RL task demonstrations or comparison to using learned representations directly

strengths: Comprehensive experimental design with custom benchmark environments where ground-truth MAD is known, enabling precise quantitative evaluation across diverse MDP characteristics (stochastic/deterministic, discrete/continuous, symmetric/asymmetric)
Sound theoretical grounding with Theorem 1 characterizing MAD as a constrained optimization problem, and clear derivation connecting the idealized formulation to practical learning objectives
First systematic exploration of asymmetric distance metrics (quasimetrics) for MAD learning, with properly proved properties (triangle inequality, positive homogeneity)

Thorough empirical evaluation with multiple metrics (Spearman/Pearson correlation, Ratio CV), extensive ablations on key hyperparameters and design choices, and practical demonstration through downstream planning tasks
Excellent reproducibility documentation including implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, environment descriptions, and promised code release
weaknesses: Narrow downstream task evaluation limited to random-shooting MPC with true environment simulator; lacks validation on actual goal-conditioned RL, reward shaping, or option discovery tasks mentioned as motivating applications

Ground-truth MAD for continuous environments (PointMaze, AntMaze) obtained via discretization + Floyd-Warshall; paper provides no sensitivity analysis, discretization granularity justification, or evidence that this approximation is valid, undermining quantitative claims (e.g., perfect 1.00 ± 0.00 correlations are suspect)

Incremental novelty building heavily on PlanDist with quasimetrics and improved loss functions, but lacking deep insights; the superiority of the simple quasimetric over complex alternatives (IQE, Wide Norm) appears empirical/domain-specific with no principled design guidance

TDMadDist consistently underperforms MadDist across all environments despite incorporating TD bootstrapping, contradicting theoretical intuition; paper dismisses this with vague reference to 'specific parametrization' without deeper analysis

Experimental design concerns: different baselines use different architectures/hyperparameters; evaluation fairness unclear; variance overlaps in some results suggest differences may not be significant; PlanDist-Simple results inconsistently reported
Missing ablations to isolate contribution of asymmetric metrics from improved loss functions (comparing PlanDist-Simple with equivalent objective would clarify this)
No theoretical analysis: lacking convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or formal justification for design choices; no guidance for extending method to new domains

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real limitation of prior work (asymmetric distances for MAD)
Correct theoretical characterization of MAD as unique pointwise maximal solution to constrained optimization (Theorem 1)
Comprehensive benchmark design with known ground-truth MAD across diverse MDP characteristics (stochastic/deterministic, discrete/continuous, symmetric/asymmetric)
Multiple complementary evaluation metrics (Spearman, Pearson correlations, Ratio CV) providing diverse perspectives on distance quality
Thorough implementation documentation (Tables 2-6) and promised code release supporting reproducibility
Extensive ablation studies (Appendices E-F) examining latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size, and constraint horizon
weaknesses: Limited core algorithmic novelty: MadDist is incremental over PlanDist (Steccanella & Jonsson, 2022) with primarily a scale-invariant loss and contrastive term; TDMadDist simply applies standard RL bootstrapping

Trivial quasimetric contribution: d_simple is merely a weighted combination of max/sum reductions of coordinate-wise differences; ablations show only modest improvements over IQE/Wide Norm (0.93-1.00 vs 0.87-0.95 Pearson correlation) with no principled justification for the design

Absence of theoretical analysis of proposed methods: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or approximation error analysis showing how closely MadDist/TDMadDist approximate the ideal MAD

Severely limited downstream application evaluation: only random-shooting MPC planning evaluated (deliberately weak planner); near-perfect success rates (1.00±0.00) in many settings suggest insufficient task difficulty; no evaluation of policy learning, reward shaping, or option discovery tasks cited in introduction

Incomplete treatment of stochastic environments: no clear characterization of what quantity is learned in truly stochastic domains; NoisyGridWorld adds observation noise rather than action stochasticity; conclusion acknowledges Stochastic Shortest Path Distance as future work

Weak baseline comparisons: missing symmetric version of MadDist (L2 distance) to isolate quasimetric benefits; PlanDist-Simple results show algorithmic changes contribute significantly (e.g., AntMaze 0.39→0.80); limited set of only 4 baselines

Modest empirical improvements: Pearson correlations often overlap between methods (0.70-1.00 range); CV metric improvements inconsistent; modest planning gains don't overcome limited scope of evaluation

High hyperparameter complexity with insufficient justification: numerous settings (w_r, w_c, d_max, H_c) appear arbitrary; unclear whether these are environment-specific or how practitioners would select them without ground-truth MAD
Missing critical ablations: no isolation of contrastive loss L_r contribution; no computational cost comparison; no analysis of when asymmetry provides substantial benefits vs. marginal improvements

Limited scope of evaluation environments: simple grid worlds for basic tests; OGBench environments approximate ground-truth via discretized Floyd-Warshall (approximation error not quantified); no image-based or large-scale real-world evaluation

strengths: Strong theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 elegantly establishes MAD as the unique pointwise maximal solution to a constrained optimization problem; systematic derivation from intractable formulation to practical algorithms

Principled treatment of asymmetric distances via quasimetrics, addressing a key limitation of prior symmetric metric approaches; well-motivated for environments with irreversible dynamics (one-way paths, key-door mechanisms)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with direct metric assessment enabled by known ground-truth MAD (rare in RL), spanning diverse MDP characteristics (discrete/continuous state spaces, deterministic/stochastic dynamics, noisy observations, symmetric/asymmetric transitions)

Consistent empirical improvements across all environments with perfect or near-perfect performance on downstream goal-reaching tasks, including challenging scenarios (trajectory stitching, random exploration data)
Transparent implementation with extensive implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, and environment documentation supporting reproducibility
Practical simplicity: the simple quasimetric dsimple is computationally efficient and outperforms more complex alternatives (IQE, Wide Norm) in ablations
Useful benchmark contribution: diverse suite of environments with computable ground-truth MAD enables systematic evaluation of distance learning methods
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: MadDist and TDMadDist are incremental extensions of prior work (PlanDist 2022), combining scale-invariant loss, contrastive regularization, and quasimetric support without substantial conceptual advances

Lack of theoretical analysis for learning algorithms: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or approximation error analysis connecting practical objectives to true MAD; no analysis of how trajectory-based upper bounds approximate true constraints

Ground-truth MAD approximation in continuous spaces via discretization + Floyd-Warshall is not exact; sensitivity to discretization granularity is not analyzed, weakening claims of 'known ground truth'

Limited downstream application scope: only goal-reaching planning evaluated despite motivating policy learning, reward shaping, and option discovery applications; planning uses true simulator (impractical), and trajectory sampling for AntMaze may favor the method
TDMadDist underperformance in many settings is inadequately explained; limited guidance on when to use which variant despite proposing both algorithms
Quasimetric design (dsimple combining max and mean of positive differences) lacks deep theoretical justification; appears somewhat ad-hoc despite strong empirical performance
Scalability properties unknown: all experiments on relatively low-dimensional problems (≤29D) and moderate horizons (≤1000 steps); behavior on high-dimensional or very long-horizon tasks unclear

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Hilbert baseline uses specific algorithm (IQL + HER) making it hard to isolate metric factors; no comparison to learned value functions or other state abstraction methods
Missing analyses: sensitivity to noise level, impact of exploration policy bias, behavior with partially observable states; constraint enforcement beyond Hc horizon is implicit and not analyzed
